questions.q: What is Pappachi's profession before retirement, and what was his highest rank?
questions.a: Pappachi (John Ipe) was an Imperial Entomologist at the Pusa Institute, and by the year he retired he had risen to a rank equivalent to Director. A wrong answer (e.g., "he was a pickle-maker" or "he was a doctor") reveals the student has not read the basic factual details of the text and cannot ground analysis in evidence.

questions.q: In your own words, explain why Pappachi resents Mammachi's pickle-making success.
questions.a: Pappachi resents Mammachi's success because it threatens his sense of superiority and traditional gender roles; as a retired high-ranking official, he considers pickle-making beneath him and cannot tolerate his wife gaining attention and independence. A wrong answer that focuses only on "he is jealous" without linking to his pride, status, and patriarchal mindset shows superficial comprehension.

questions.q: Find two specific actions Pappachi takes to humiliate Mammachi publicly, and explain what each action reveals about his character.
questions.a: 1. He sits on the verandah sewing buttons that aren't missing onto his shirts to create the impression Mammachi neglects him — reveals his manipulative pettiness and desire to control public perception. 2. He buys the skyblue Plymouth and forbids anyone else from using it — reveals his need to assert dominance and exact "revenge" through material possession. A wrong answer that lists actions without explaining the psychological insight shows inability to move from evidence to inference.

questions.q: Compare Pappachi's reaction to the moth discovery being named after someone else with his reaction to retirement. What common psychological pattern do they reveal?
questions.a: Both events wound Pappachi's pride because they deny him the recognition and status he believes he deserves; retirement strips his official identity, and the moth naming denies his scientific legacy. The pattern: his self-worth is entirely dependent on external validation (titles, names, ranks), and when that validation fails, he responds with silent resentment and destructive behaviour rather than introspection. A wrong answer that treats the two events as unrelated misses the core thematic link between colonial bureaucracy and personal identity.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Pappachi is a villain with no redeeming qualities." Use textual evidence to support your judgment.
questions.a: The statement is too simplistic. While Pappachi commits domestic violence and emotional abuse (villainous acts), the text invites sympathy by showing his vulnerability: the "ignominy of retirement", the moth disappointment, the Vienna photograph of his younger hopeful self. Arundhati Roy portrays him as a product of colonial hierarchy and patriarchal conditioning — a tragic figure whose flaws are magnified by systemic forces. A good evaluation acknowledges both his agency in cruelty and the context that shapes him. A wrong answer that simply agrees or disagrees without nuance fails the evaluative demand.

questions.q: Write a 100-word diary entry from Pappachi's perspective on the night he smashes his rocking chair, capturing his inner turmoil without justifying his violence.
questions.a: A strong entry would show his rage at Chacko's interference, his humiliation at being physically overpowered by his son, the collapse of his authority, and the moth's "pernicious ghost" haunting him — all while maintaining his voice: formal, proud, bitter. Example opening: "The boy — my son — twisted my arm like I was a common coolie. In my own study. After all I built..." A poor entry would either excuse the violence ("Mammachi provoked me") or turn him into a cartoon villain ("I hate everyone"), missing the complex pride and fragility.
